source.title: X-SYS: A Reference Architecture for Interactive Explanation Systems
source.authors: T. Labarta; Nhi Y. Hoang; Maximilian Dreyer; Jim Berend; Oleg Hein; Jackie Ma; W. Samek; S. Lapuschkin

record.tranche_reason: SemanticLens uses component-level semantic search and activation steering as explanation tools and reports illustrative outcomes, but does not test the neuron-interpretability claims or their stated measures.
record.gate_note: The paper gives illustrative SemanticLens results: semantic search aligns components with text queries, and suppressing one component changes a prediction. These do not measure neuron-pole job shares, held-out explanation faithfulness, automated explanation scores, or the sufficiency of attribution graphs. Statements about architecture quality attributes are not systematic measurements. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper presents a reference architecture for explanation systems (X-SYS) and one implementation, SemanticLens. It uses component-level semantic search and activation steering as tools and shows illustrative examples. It reports no share of interpretable neurons, no held-out faithfulness of explanations, no automated explanation scores, and no attribution-graph sufficiency result, so none of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors present X-SYS as a reference architecture organized around four quality attributes (scalability, traceability, responsiveness, adaptability) with five components, instantiated via SemanticLens. They state that generality, practical benefit and systematic measurement of the quality attributes remain unvalidated.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes and instantiates an interactive explanation-system architecture; it does not reproduce the original neuron-audit or neuron-explanation methods.

fits_no_version.finding: In WhyLesionCLIP, suppressing component #30496 (m = -1), which had the highest attribution for text markings, reverted a text-induced misclassification to 'melanoma'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Suppressing a single component that responds to a spurious artifact can correct a Clever Hans prediction in the illustrated case.

fits_no_version.finding: Semantic search for 'pasta' in ResNet50 returned component #858 ('carbonara', similarity 1.00) and #1268 ('dough', 0.74).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Text-query semantic search can retrieve vision-model components whose labels align with the query.

record.problems: The paper describes a single implementation and explicitly says generality and practical benefit are unvalidated. It also says systematic measurements of the four quality attributes have not been proposed. The component-level examples are illustrative; no sample sizes, controls, or uncertainty estimates are reported for them.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B pole-share audit: one main job, two related jobs, not yet understood.
Shares across other language models, dense and MoE, and across scale.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron; pose detection; recursive generalization versus superposition.
Effect of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons.
Neuron-based attribution graphs explaining behaviour without a replacement model.
Whether explanations that fit activating examples predict firing on other inputs.
Simulation-based automated scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is a systems and architecture paper. The neuron-level examples are demonstrations of the tool, not evidence on whether neurons are monosemantic or whether their explanations are faithful. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B pole-share estimate and its breakdown into one job, two related jobs, and not-yet-understood poles.
Similar shares across models, architectures, and scales.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Whether architecture, regularization, or tools explain interpretability rates, and the stated estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Whether attribution graphs using a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model or its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples fail to predict firing on other examples.
Automated scores of neuron explanations on new text, including comparisons across explainer models.
